writing.prompt:
Part I Writing (30 minutes)

Directions: For this part, you are allowed 30 minutes to write an essay on the importance of a sense of responsibility. You can base your essay on the following three aspects: social responsibility, family responsibility, or responsibility in one's community. You can cite examples to illustrate your point. You should write at least 150 words but no more than 200 words.
writing.ideas: 审题思路:现象分析类,论述某一层面责任感的重要性。建议选「社会责任」,素材最丰富(志愿者活动、环保行为、公共秩序)。三段式:① 首段定义责任感并指出它是个人成熟的标志;② 中间段从两个层面展开:对他人的直接影响(举例:社区志愿服务/疫情期间互助)与对自身的反哺(责任感带来信任与机会);③ 结尾升华:责任感不是负担而是参与世界的方式,呼吁从小事做起。
writing.model:
A sense of responsibility is what turns an individual into a reliable member of society. Among its many forms, social responsibility matters most, because it connects private lives with the public good.
Its importance first shows in what we do for others. When university students volunteer to tutor children in migrant schools, or when residents organise to separate rubbish for recycling, the benefit flows outward to people who may never know their names. Yet responsibility also rewards those who practise it. A young person known for keeping promises and finishing what they start naturally earns trust, and trust opens doors that talent alone cannot. In this sense, responsibility is not a burden imposed from outside but an investment in one's own character.
Of course, responsibility cannot be built in grand gestures alone. It grows from small, repeated choices—showing up on time, admitting mistakes, finishing the boring part of a group project. A society is strong not because it contains heroes, but because it contains millions of people who take their own small duties seriously.
writing.notes: 亮点:① 首句 reliably member 定义式开头,简洁有力;② 中间段双线论证:利他(志愿者例子)+ 利己(信任打开机会之门),打破「责任只是付出」的片面;③ 结尾 small, repeated choices 落到可操作层面,并用 not heroes but millions 收束升华。加分表达:the public good, flows outward, imposed from outside, takes their own small duties seriously。

listening.intro:
Questions 1 to 4 are based on the conversation you have just heard.

【听力原文】
W: Mark, you joined three clubs in your first month. How is that going?
M: Honestly, terribly. I am spread so thin that I contribute nothing meaningful anywhere.
W: So why did you sign up for so many?
M: I thought more clubs would look better on graduate-school applications.
W: Admissions officers see through that. What they look for is depth: a role where you actually changed something.
M: That makes sense. I have decided to keep the debate club and drop the other two.
W: Good choice. You could even run for a committee position there and organise an inter-school tournament.
M: That would be a real achievement. Let me talk to the advisor this week.
listening.questions:
1. What is the man's problem?
A) He cannot decide which club to join.
B) He is doing poorly in his studies.
C) He has joined too many clubs.
D) He was rejected by the debate club.

2. Why did the man join many clubs at first?
A) He wanted to make more friends.
B) He thought it would help his applications.
C) His advisor recommended it.
D) He wanted to win competitions.

3. What do admissions officers look for, according to the woman?
A) The number of clubs joined.
B) Leadership titles.
C) Depth of involvement.
D) Academic grades only.

4. What has the man decided to do?
A) Keep only the debate club.
B) Quit all clubs.
C) Join two more clubs.
D) Become a club advisor.
listening.analysis:
1. C。男士说 joined three clubs,spread so thin that I contribute nothing meaningful,问题是加入太多。
2. B。他原以为 more clubs would look better on graduate-school applications。
3. C。女士说招生官看重深度(What they look for is depth),即真正做成事的投入。
4. A。男士决定 keep the debate club and drop the other two。

listening.intro:
Questions 5 to 7 are based on the passage you have just heard.

【听力原文】
Reading used to be a marathon; today, for many people, it has become a series of sprints. Psychologists studying reading habits have found that constant scrolling on screens trains the brain to expect a new stimulus every few seconds. When readers then open a long article, they often find their attention drifting after just a few paragraphs—not because the article is dull, but because their brains have been reconditioned.
The consequences go beyond reading. In one study, students who read a chapter on paper scored significantly higher on comprehension questions than students who read the same chapter on a screen filled with hyperlinks. The paper readers remembered the argument's structure; the screen readers remembered scattered facts.
Researchers stress that the effect is reversible. Setting aside thirty minutes a day for slow, linear reading gradually restores the patience that deep texts demand. The muscle of attention, like any other, weakens with disuse and strengthens with training.
listening.questions:
5. What have psychologists found about constant scrolling?
A) It improves reading speed.
B) It makes people prefer long articles.
C) It conditions the brain to expect frequent stimuli.
D) It has no effect on attention.

6. How did paper readers differ from screen readers in the study?
A) They read much faster.
B) They remembered the argument's structure.
C) They preferred hyperlinks.
D) They scored lower on facts.

7. What do researchers say about the effect?
A) It is permanent.
B) It can be reversed by slow reading.
C) It only affects young people.
D) It improves with training apps.
listening.analysis:
5. C。短文指出不断滑动屏幕训练大脑每隔几秒就期待新刺激(expect a new stimulus every few seconds)。
6. B。研究中纸面阅读者记住了论证结构,屏幕阅读者只记得零散事实。
7. B。研究者强调这种影响可逆,每天慢读三十分钟可恢复耐心(reversible / restores the patience)。

listening.intro:
Questions 8 to 10 are based on the lecture you have just heard.

【听力原文】
Good morning, everyone. Today we will look at a communication model that has helped thousands of couples and workplaces reduce conflict: nonviolent communication, or NVC, developed by Marshall Rosenberg in the 1960s.
The core idea of NVC is surprisingly simple: most conflicts escalate not because people disagree, but because of how they express disagreement. A sentence like "You never listen to me!" triggers defence within a second. Rosenberg proposed replacing such judgements with a four-step formula: observation, feeling, need and request. Instead of blaming, you describe what happened ("When I spoke just now, you looked at your phone"), name your feeling ("I feel frustrated"), identify your need ("because I need to feel heard"), and make a clear request ("Could you put the phone down while we talk?").
What makes this formula powerful is that it separates observation from evaluation. The same event—"you arrived at eight"—can be stated neutrally or judgementally, and the choice determines whether the conversation becomes a fight. In workshops, participants who practise the formula for just two weeks report that their arguments become shorter and their resolutions come faster. I would encourage you to try it in your next disagreement and notice the difference.
listening.questions:
8. What is the core idea of nonviolent communication?
A) Conflict comes from disagreement itself.
B) Conflict escalates because of how people express disagreement.
C) Couples should avoid all arguments.
D) Judgements help resolve conflicts.

9. Which of the following is NOT a step in Rosenberg's formula?
A) Observation.
B) Evaluation.
C) Feeling.
D) Request.

10. What did workshop participants report after practising the formula?
A) They stopped disagreeing.
B) Their arguments became shorter.
C) They avoided difficult topics.
D) They needed two weeks to see no change.
listening.analysis:
8. B。讲座核心观点:冲突升级多因表达方式而非分歧本身(most conflicts escalate not because people disagree, but because of how they express disagreement)。
9. B。四步公式是 observation, feeling, need, request,不含 evaluation;讲座还特意强调要把观察与评价分开。
10. B。工作坊参与者练习两周后报告争论变短、解决更快(arguments become shorter and resolutions come faster)。

reading.title: Why Remote Work Rewrites the Rules of Trust
reading.passage:
For decades, the unwritten contract of office life was simple: presence equalled productivity. Managers could see who arrived early, who stayed late, and who chatted too long by the coffee machine. Remote work has dismantled that contract almost overnight. When employees log in from kitchens and co-working spaces, visibility disappears, and with it, the old proxy for commitment. What remains is something more fragile and more valuable: trust.
Research on distributed teams suggests that the transition is harder for managers than for staff. A study tracking two thousand hybrid workers found that supervisors consistently rated remote employees as slightly less productive, even when objective output—code committed, articles published, tickets closed—showed the opposite. The gap, psychologists argue, comes from a cognitive bias called "mere exposure": we instinctively trust people we see often, regardless of their results. Managing by results rather than by sightings requires unlearning a habit that is older than the office itself.
For employees, remote work shifts a different burden: self-management. Without a commute framing the day or colleagues modelling focus, the boundary between work and life blurs, and some people quietly work longer hours than they ever did on site. Successful remote workers, surveys show, treat discipline as a designed system rather than a virtue: fixed start times, a dedicated workspace, and a hard stop in the evening. Technology, it turns out, was the easy part of working from home; the hard part is rewriting the habits that offices used to enforce for free.
reading.questions:
1. What was the "unwritten contract" of office life?
A) Overtime was rewarded.
B) Presence equalled productivity.
C) Coffee breaks built trust.
D) Managers worked remotely.

2. What did the study of two thousand hybrid workers find?
A) Remote employees produced less output.
B) Supervisors rated remote workers lower despite equal output.
C) Managers preferred remote work.
D) Objective output was hard to measure.

3. What does "mere exposure" refer to in the passage?
A) Trusting people we see often.
B) Judging people by results.
C) Working longer hours.
D) Meeting colleagues frequently.

4. What burden does remote work shift to employees?
A) Managing their own time and focus.
B) Supervising their managers.
C) Commuting longer distances.
D) Designing office spaces.

5. What do successful remote workers treat discipline as?
A) A natural virtue.
B) A designed system.
C) An office rule.
D) A technological tool.
reading.analysis:
1. B。第一段 unwritten contract 指 presence equalled productivity(在场即生产力)。
2. B。第二段:即便客观产出相当甚至更高,主管仍给远程员工打更低分, ratings 与 objective output 相反。
3. A。心理学家用「纯粹接触效应」解释:本能地更信任常见到的人,与其成果无关。
4. A。第三段:远程办公把自我管理的负担转移给员工(self-management,时间与专注力)。
5. B。末句:成功的远程工作者把纪律当作设计好的系统(a designed system)而非个人美德。

translation.prompt:
请将以下中文段落翻译成英文:

随着中国经济的快速发展和国际影响力的提升,全球范围内学习汉语的人数持续增长。目前,超过一百个国家将汉语教学纳入本国教育体系,各类孔子学院成为传播语言文化的重要平台。汉语热的背后,既有经贸往来带来的实际需求,也体现了世界对中国历史与文化的浓厚兴趣。语言是沟通的桥梁,学习汉语为各国人民了解中国打开了新的窗口。
translation.reference: With the rapid growth of China's economy and its rising international influence, the number of people learning Chinese around the world keeps increasing. Today, more than one hundred countries have incorporated Chinese teaching into their national education systems, and Confucius Institutes have become important platforms for spreading the language and culture. Behind this enthusiasm for Chinese lies both the practical demand generated by economic exchanges and a keen interest in China's history and culture. Language is a bridge of communication, and learning Chinese opens a new window for people of all countries to understand China.
translation.notes: 要点:①「国际影响力的提升」译为 its rising international influence,用形容词 rising 比 improving 更自然;②「纳入教育体系」用 incorporate... into their national education systems;③「汉语热」译为 this enthusiasm for Chinese,避免直译;④「沟通的桥梁」固定表达 a bridge of communication;⑤ 注意 with 独立主格结构开头的句式变换,避免全句主语都是「人数」。
